abstract: Significance The spread of mobile genetic elements within and between the genomes of diverse organisms has greatly impacted biology across the tree of life. Inteins are an enigmatic type of mobile genetic element capable of self-splicing at the protein level. While inteins are generally rare in eukaryotes, we show that three strains of the recently described eukaryotic microbe Anaeramoeba have many dozens of inteins encoded in their nuclear genomes. Genomic investigation shows that Anaeramoeba ’s inteins were likely acquired by lateral transfer from viruses and bacteria and subsequently spread to many different genomic locations via allelic and, possibly, nonallelic homing. The promiscuous nature of inteins in Anaeramoeba makes them promising substrates for genetic engineering and biotechnological applications.
methods:
Materials and Methods
Intein Searches.
Two methods were used to detect inteins in the three
Anaeramoeba
predicted proteomes. First, BLAST (
50
) v2.9.0 was used (e-value <= 1e−5) with the inteins published in InBase and those described by Green et al. (
12
) as queries. Second, searches with Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) were performed using Hmmer (
51
) v. 3.3 using HMM profiles built using the N-terminal and C-terminal splicing domains of reference inteins (smart 00305, smart00306, PS50817, PS50818, PF14623, PF13403, and cd00081). Inteins detected during this first round of searching were used as queries for additional BLASTp searches. tBLASTn was used to detect potential pseudogenized inteins using the same queries as previously as well as the newly extracted complete set of
Anaeramoeba
full-length inteins.
Intein Splicing.
The splicing of inteins in
Anaeramoeba
was investigated experimentally using a combination of shotgun proteomics (
A. flamelloides
BUSSELTON2) and GFP-based in vitro expression analyses in
E. coli
(
A. ignava
BMAN). Detailed methodologies can be found in
SI Appendix
, section 2
. Proteomic data can be found in the PRoteomics IDEntifications (PRIDE) database (awaiting final access links).
Phylogenetic Analysis.
Unless specified otherwise, intein sequences were aligned with mafft (
52
) v7.407 using default parameters, sites were selected with bmge (
53
) v1.12 with the -m BLOSUM30 parameter, and IQ-TREE (
54
) v1.6.3 was used to reconstruct phylogenies with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates (
55
) under the C20+G4 mixture model.
Sequence Similarity Network.
Anaeramoeba
inteins were used as queries to retrieve homologous inteins from the
nr
database (2020). For each intein, the 25 best matching inteins were selected. The EFI EST software (
56
) was used to construct the network from the splicing domains of retrieved inteins using default parameters. For filtration into clusters, a threshold score corresponding to an average of 30% identity was used, which is an approximate threshold by which allelic and nonallelic inteins can be discriminated (
9
). The resulting network was visualized and edited with Cytoscape (
57
).
HE Domain Detection.
Two methods were used to detect HE domains, Interproscan v5.32-71.0 and HMM searches. In the latter case, HMM profiles constructed from alignments of HEs in the PFAM (PF00961, PF03161, PF05204, PF09062, PF10298, PF14527, PF14528, PF01223, PF01844, PF02945, PF03165, PF04231, PF05315, PF05551, PF05766, PF06147, PF07510, PF09230, PF12639, PF13391, PF13392, PF13395, PF13930, PF14279, PF14410, PF14411, PF14412, PF14414, PF16784, PF16786, and PF18275) and Prosite (PS50164) databases were used as queries.
DNA Replication and Repair Systems.
One hundred thirty-one human and yeast proteins from the replisome and NHEJ, HR, BER, NER, and MMR DNA repair pathways were used to identify their best PANTHER v15 family HMM model using PANTHER Score tool (
58
). These HMM models were then used to identify homologs in the predicted proteomes of the three
Anaeramoeba
genomes as well as those of
T. vaginalis
,
M. exilis
,
C. frisia
,
C. membranifera
,
K. bialata
,
G. intestinalis
WB,
S. salmonicida
,
N. gruberi
, and
D. discoideum
. Query proteins and retrieved homologs were then aligned with a random taxonomic sample from the same PANTHER family of interest for ortholog validation. Alignments were trimmed and subjected to phylogenetic reconstructions similarly to those described in ref.
46
.

body:
Inteins are internal protein elements capable of catalyzing their own excision (
1
,
2
). Analogous to self-splicing mRNA introns, intein self-splicing results in peptide bond formation between the amino (N)- and carboxyl (C)-terminal exteins and reconstitution of the mature host protein. Many inteins contain a homing endonuclease (HE) domain (
3
) that facilitates their mobility at the DNA level. Homing begins with the creation of a double-strand break in an intein-free allele by the HE encoded by an intein-donor allele. Using the endogenous homologous recombination pathway, the cleaved allele then recombines with the intein-donor allele, resulting in intein spread (
4
,
5
). This process also likely underlies how inteins move between the genomes of different organisms by lateral gene transfer (LGT) (
6
–
8
). HE-mediated allelic specificity means that intein coding regions found at the same location tend to share more sequence similarity to one another than to those in different locations (
9
).
Inteins were initially described in the Vacuolar ATPase (VMA) of
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
(
10
,
11
), and the subsequent growth of sequence databases facilitated the systematic search for inteins in bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, and viruses (
12
,
13
). Inteins are more abundant in prokaryotes, with 25% of bacterial and 50% of archaeal genomes encoding at least one intein (
13
). While prokaryotic inteins are hosted by many different proteins (
13
), >60% of intein-containing proteins in prokaryotes are involved in DNA replication, recombination, and repair. One possible explanation for this bias is that the expression of inteins in concert with DNA repair enzymes reduces the damaging effects of nonspecific HE activity, thereby reducing selection against intein spread (
3
). It may also facilitate intein spread by ensuring that the recipient (intein-minus) allele is in an open chromatin state at the same time as the homing enzymes are active (
3
,
14
). Another factor is that DNA replication, recombination, and repair genes are prevalent in phage genomes (
13
,
15
–
17
), which could facilitate phage-mediated intein spread (
13
,
18
). Inteins generally reside within evolutionarily conserved regions of proteins such as active sites, DNA-binding sites, and ligand-binding motifs (
13
,
14
,
18
). This nonrandom distribution is thought to hinder intein loss, as imprecise deletions of the intein sequence would negatively impact host protein function (
18
). Given that such sites are highly conserved across species, it could also facilitate HE-mediated homing and LGT of inteins between distantly related organisms (
18
). Interestingly, research suggests that some inteins have been exapted to the benefit of their host organisms as “environmental sensors,” with conditional splicing playing a role in the regulation of host protein expression (
19
,
20
).
The intein distribution landscape in eukaryotes differs greatly from prokaryotes. A recent analysis revealed 257 inteins residing in the nuclear or chloroplast genomes of 231 eukaryotes (
12
). These inteins were restricted primarily to unicellular species and to a much smaller array of proteins than in prokaryotes. Indeed, no nucleus-encoded DNA processing proteins have been reported to host inteins. Fungal
Pre
-
mRNA
-
processing factor 8
(Prp8) and VMA are the most common hosts of nuclear inteins, followed by RNA polymerases (RNApol) in several fungi and some amoebozoans. Here we report the existence of a remarkably high number of inteins in the nuclear genomes of three strains of
Anaeramoeba
, a recently characterized genus of unicellular anaerobic eukaryotes belonging to the Metamonada, a eukaryotic “supergroup” noteworthy in having mitochondrion-related organelles with metabolisms adapted to low-oxygen environments (
21
–
23
). Analysis of their peculiar intein distribution profiles provides important insights into the origins and spread of inteins within and between the genomes of eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses.
Results
Inteins Are Abundant in
Anaeramoeba
.
Preliminary investigation of three
Anaeramoeba
nuclear genomes—
A. ignava
strain BMAN,
A. flamelloides
strain BUSSELTON2, and
A. flamelloides
strain SCHOONER1 (
23
)—revealed the presence of numerous putative intein-encoding regions. Using BLAST- and hidden Markov model–based approaches, we performed a systematic survey of the
Anaeramoeba
proteins using inteins from InBase and previous studies (
12
,
24
). We predicted 103, 45, and 47 complete inteins in
A. ignava
,
A. flamelloides
(BUSSELTON2), and
A. flamelloides
(SCHOONER1), respectively (
Table 1
), far exceeding the highest number found in any other organism sequenced to date (16 in bacteria, 15 in archaea, and four nucleus-encoded inteins in the opisthokont
Capsaspora owczarzaki
) (
13
). We also found pseudogenized inteins (
SI Appendix
, section 1
) but no “split” inteins (i.e., those undergoing
trans
-splicing). In
A. ignava
strain BMAN, 15 proteins were found to have two or more inteins; in BUSSELTON2 and SCHOONER1, three and four proteins have two or more inteins, respectively. Remarkably, the BMAN intron splicing protein Prp8 has five inteins, four at previously described sites [Prp8-a,-b,-d and -e (
25
)] and one at a novel site (Prp8-f) located in the RNAse H domain (residues AKWK/TAEE;
Dataset S1
). In addition to Prp8, one of the BMAN dynein paralogs hosts three inteins, as do the MCM6 and MCM8 proteins. A maximum of four inteins was previously described for a single protein (
26
), although we also found other instances of four inteins per protein in taxonomically diverse archaeal MCM proteins; i.e., in National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) reference sequences:
WP_083500658.1
,
WP_048152640
,
WP_014557079.1
.

Splicing was confirmed for three
Anaeramoeba
inteins using a combination of shotgun proteomics and in vitro experiments. Approximately 4,000 proteins were detected in
A. flamelloides
BUSSELTON2 using nanoLC-MS/MS, although peptides diagnostic of splicing (i.e., those mapping to intein-extein boundaries) were rare. Two inteins in DNA-directed RNA polymerase 2 subunit 2 (RPB2) were nevertheless shown to be spliced out of their native extein host (
SI Appendix
, section 2
). One of the three predicted inteins in the
A. ignava
BMAN activating signal cointegrator 1 complex 3 (g14419.t1) protein was also shown in vitro to splice out of a GFP-intein construct expressed in
Escherichia coli
(
Fig. 1
and
SI Appendix
, section 2
). This intein is noteworthy in that it is a singleton (it shows no obvious similarity to inteins described in other organisms; see below). Combined with these experimental data and the fact that many of the predicted
Anaeramoeba
inteins reside in presumed-to-be essential proteins (see below), examination of splicing domain sequences (
SI Appendix
, section 3
) suggests that most inteins identified herein are capable of splicing.

Exceptional Functional Diversity of
Anaeramoeba
Intein-Containing Proteins.
We used the Eukaryotic Orthologous Groups of proteins (KOG) database to assign a KOG and functional category to each
Anaeramoeba
intein-containing protein.
Anaeramoeba
inteins reside in 55 different KOGs (given that some proteins host several inteins and some inteins are found in species-specific paralogs, the number of unique KOGs is less than the total number of inteins). In contrast, other known eukaryotic nuclear inteins are restricted to 15 different KOGs, 13 of which were described by Green et al. (
12
) [we detected two additional intein-containing KOGs in the green alga
Chloropicon primus
: DNApol delta KOG0969 and zeta KOG0968 (protein accessions
QDZ18123.1
and
QDZ21998
, respectively)].
Anaeramoeba
intein-containing proteins corresponding to intein-bearing KOGs in other eukaryotes include (but are not limited to) Prp8 (BMAN, BUSSELTON2, and SCHOONER1), VMA (BMAN only), DNA-directed RNA polymerase 2 subunit 2 (RPB2) (BMAN, BUSSELTON2, and SCHOONER1), and Transcription initiation factor 5B (BMAN only). Numerous
Anaeramoeba
proteins with inteins have an intein-containing homolog in archaea, bacteria, or both (29, 12, and 12 for BMAN, BUSSELTON2, and SCHOONER1, respectively). Additionally, several intein-bearing proteins in
Anaeramoeba
have intein-containing homologs in
Nucleocytoviricota
, namely Lon proteases, DNApol alpha, delta, and epsilon, and the largest and second-largest subunit of RNA polymerase (the two latter proteins were previously the only intein-bearing proteins reported in both eukaryotes and viruses). The remaining KOGs (18 in BMAN and three each in BUSSELTON2 and SCHOONER1) represent novel host proteins (
Table 1
and
Dataset S1
).
While the functional distribution of nucleus-encoded intein host proteins in eukaryotes differs from that of prokaryotes (
12
,
13
), the
Anaeramoeba
profile exhibits both eukaryotic and prokaryotic signatures (
Fig. 2
). For example, the functional category RNA processing and modification (A) (which includes Prp8 and Prp16) is well represented in the intein-containing host proteins of
Anaeramoeba
and other eukaryotes but not in prokaryotes. Similarly, category K (Transcription) is well represented in
Anaeramoeba
and other eukaryotes but is a minor category in prokaryotic host proteins. However, most
Anaeramoeba
inteins are found in proteins belonging to category L—Replication, recombination, and repair—which is a common feature of prokaryotic but not eukaryotic host proteins.

We also detected
Anaeramoeba
inteins in proteins belonging to functional categories that were not previously reported to contain intein-hosting proteins, namely Cytoskeleton (Z) and Chromatin structure and dynamics (B). Curiously, multiple
Anaeramoeba
proteins belonging to these categories were found to be invaded by inteins: two types of Dynein (Cytoplasmic dynein 1 heavy chain 1 and Dynein heavy chain 10, axonemal isoform) and one Kinesin for Cytoskeleton (Z); and two different Helicases in category B (Chromatin remodeling protein HARP/SMARCAL1 and Chromatin remodeling complex SWI/SNF, component SWI2) (
Fig. 2
). Furthermore, some of these proteins host several inteins (e.g., three in a dynein homolog of
A. ignava
). We note that these inteins are not randomly distributed within the newly identified host proteins but are instead localized to more highly conserved regions. Collectively, these results indicate that cytoskeletal and chromatin structuring proteins can be “suitable” intein hosts.
Anaeramoeba
Inteins Are Evolutionarily Diverse.
To infer the evolutionary origins of the inteins in
Anaeramoeba
, we used a sequence similarity network-based approach. This is because inteins are often so divergent in sequence that phylogenetic methods fail to yield meaningful results (
9
). This is particularly problematic when comparing nonallelic inteins, i.e., those inserted in different proteins or different regions of the same protein. Consistent with the diversity of host proteins in
Anaeramoeba
and the low sequence identity shared among the inteins themselves,
Anaeramoeba
inteins have diverse origins (
Fig. 3
). Eighteen distinct clusters linking
Anaeramoeba
inteins to those in prokaryotes, eukaryotes or viruses were inferred. This pattern is suggestive of many independent acquisitions from diverse sources, although it is impossible to discern exactly how many due to the complex nature of the network.
Fig. 3.
Anaeramoeba
inteins are evolutionarily diverse. Sequence Similarity Network (SSN) of inteins in
A. ignava
strain BMAN,
A. flamelloides
strains BUSSELTON2 and SCHOONER1, and related inteins found in public databases. The edges between the nodes are a measure of the similarity between nodes (score threshold corresponding to 30% identity on average). Anaeramoebae inteins belong to 18 different clusters corresponding to at least as many acquisition events. Some inteins do not show obvious sequence similarity with any other known inteins and are singleton or “pseudo-singleton” clusters (see main text). Inteins in viral-like sequences in eukaryotic genomes are designated EVEs (Endogenous Viral Elements). Note: “+”: HE domain detected in
Anaeramoeba
intein using one or both methods (HEs in the inteins of other organisms are not highlighted); *In orthologous site; **In homologous site.
Nine
Anaeramoeba
inteins are singletons—they show no meaningful similarity to any known inteins. Additionally, two inteins in BMAN, 16 in SCHOONER1, and 16 in BUSSELTON2 form clusters comprised only of inteins inserted at paralogous sites in recent species-specific duplicates. These are designated pseudo-singletons (
Fig. 3
). These 43 singleton/pseudo-singleton inteins reside in 13 different KOGs. Surprisingly, only one of these KOGs (AAA+-type ATPase containing a bromodomain) is not known to contain an intein in at least one other organism, while two additional KOGs have inteins but not at orthologous sites elsewhere in the tree of life [Activating Signal Cointegrator 1 Complex subunit 3 (ASC1S3) and DNApol theta/eta (POLQ)]. The 10 remaining KOGs have inteins in
Anaeramoeba
that are inserted at orthologous sites in other species. The fact that these inteins are nevertheless singletons/pseudo-singletons can be explained two ways: either they correspond to independent intein invasions of the same site by unrelated inteins, or they are allelic inteins that have diverged to the point that homology is no longer detectable (or below the threshold used for building the network). The latter scenario is the more likely explanation in at least some cases. For example, the singleton inteins hosted by the BMAN MCM8, PcrA-like helicase, CDC48 ATPase, mismatch DNA repair Msh2, RPB1, and SWI-SNF helicase proteins, as well as those in the BUSSELTON2 and SCHOONER1 MCM3 and MCM5 proteins, all show weak but consistent similarity to inteins inserted at orthologous sites in either bacteria or archaea or to other
Anaeramoeba
inteins. Also consistent with an “ancient” acquisition of the singleton/pseudo-singleton inteins is the fact that most of them lack obvious HEs, unlike most other
Anaeramoeba
inteins in the network (
Fig. 3
).
Twenty-nine
Anaeramoeba
intein-bearing proteins have intein-containing homologs in prokaryotes (in most cases, their insertion sites are homologous). Many of these inteins present in cross-kingdom homologs cluster together in our analysis (
Fig. 3
). For example, cluster 18 contains
A. flamelloides
and prokaryotic inteins inserted at homologous sites in Ribonuclease HII. Cluster 13 contains a BMAN MCM8 intein inserted at “site e” of the archaeal MCM homolog, and cluster 11 includes the BMAN MCM6 intein (insertion site c) and inteins in the homologous position of archaeal MCM proteins. Interestingly, the
Anaeramoeba
cluster 13 and 11 inteins are short—160 and 185 amino acids, respectively—consistent with ancient insertion and subsequent HE domain decay (
6
). Where these inteins arose and how they came to reside in the same site of homologous proteins in organisms from different domains of life is unclear. While
Anaeramoeba
have bacterial epibionts (
23
), we found no evidence for symbiont-to-host intein transfer as the bacterial proteomes are intein-free (
23
) (secondary intein loss in the epibionts is a formal possibility). Finally, it is worth noting that
Anaeramoeba
inteins clustering with prokaryotic inteins do not always reside in homologous proteins. For example, the
Anaeramoeba
RtcB intein does not cluster with prokaryotic RtcB inteins but rather with inteins in prokaryotic phosphoenolpyruvate synthase (PEPS). Interestingly, the intein insertion sites of BMAN RtcB and prokaryotic PEPS are vaguely similar (RtcB: FGST/CHGE; PEPS: GG[TRM]T/CHAA), raising the possibility of microhomology-mediated nonallelic homing (see below).
Seven network clusters link
Anaeramoeba
inteins to those of other eukaryotes. Several of these associations obey the so-called allelic rule, i.e., inteins hosted by orthologous proteins at orthologous sites cluster together. For example, the BMAN Prp8 intein in “site d” clusters with the Prp8 site d intein in the green alga
Bathycoccus
(
Fig. 3
, cluster 4). Other clusters are mixtures of allelic and nonallelic intein associations and, in some cases, both eukaryotic and prokaryotic host proteins (clusters 2, 17, 7, 15, 6, and 16). Interestingly, all but one of these clusters also contain viral inteins.
Viruses Mediate Intein Spread.
Eight clusters (2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15, 16, and 17) contain
Anaeramoeba
inteins and inteins from the
Nucleocytoviricota
, a phylum of large dsDNA viruses that infect eukaryotes. Five of these eight also contain inteins from at least one other eukaryote (
Fig. 3
). Together with the fact that several intein-bearing host proteins are common to
Anaeramoeba
and viruses (
Table 1
), this suggests that viruses have played a role in intein acquisition in
Anaeramoeba
and other eukaryotes (
12
,
27
), in the same way that phages have spread inteins in prokaryotes (
28
,
29
). Some viral intein-containing clusters include nonallelic
Anaeramoeba
inteins. The most striking example is cluster 15, which contains inteins in 24 different BMAN proteins and 28 sites (four sites in Prp8, two in VMA) (
Dataset S1
), as well as in nine different viral proteins. Such intein promiscuity could be the result of viral HEs with very relaxed DNA recognition specificities, which could conceivably facilitate nonallelic intein spread (
30
) (
SI Appendix
, section 8 and Fig. S14
). In the case of Anaeramoebae at least, this could be exacerbated by the DNA repair machinery using nonhomologous templates for recombination, a possibility that deserves further investigation [cluster 15 proteins include many of those in the DNA replication and repair pathways and are likely repaired by nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ); see below].
Anaeramoeba
inteins belonging to clusters 1 and 9 have atypical N- and C-terminal residues, respectively. Crucially, both features are also found in viruses (in phages for cluster 1 and
Nucleocytoviricota
for cluster 9), (
SI Appendix
, sections 4 and 5
), once again suggesting that viruses contribute to the diversification of intein alleles. Another remarkable feature of
Anaeramoeba
cluster 1 inteins is that they appear to be “Class 3” inteins, which have thus far only been described in bacteria and phages (
29
,
31
,
32
). These inteins are also found in several unrelated protein hosts, which is consistent with nonallelic spread (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
).
Virus-mediated lateral transfer of intein-containing host proteins might also explain the origins and spread of inteins in eukaryotes. We detected previously undescribed inteins in
Klebsormidium nitens
(Viridiplantae),
Tetrabaena socialis
(Viridiplantae), a multicellular alga (
33
), and
Honda fermentalgiana
(Labyrinthulomycetes), some of which appeared to reside in DNApol proteins; this has not been reported previously in eukaryotes. Detailed investigation revealed that the intein host proteins in
K. nitens
,
H. fermentalgiana,
and
T. socialis
are in fact viral-like DNA polymerases whose genes reside on bona fide nuclear scaffolds (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
). The presence of viral genes in eukaryotic nuclear chromosomes has been documented previously (
34
–
36
), including in
K. nitens
(
37
) and
T. socialis
(
38
), where they have acquired spliceosomal introns (
37
,
38
). While LGT has played a role in the evolution of
Anaeramoeba
genomes (
23
), none of the intein-hosting proteins in the three strains analyzed herein are of obvious viral ancestry, even though some of the inteins themselves appear to be. Regardless, LGT of intein-bearing host proteins from viruses is a potential avenue for allelic and nonallelic homing into eukaryotic genes.
Intragenomic Mobility of
Anaeramoeba
Inteins.
The BUSSELTON2 and SCHOONER1 strains of
A. flamelloides
share recent common ancestry (
23
); it is thus not surprising that their inteins share high percentages of amino acid identity, reside in the same sites in orthologous proteins, and cluster together in our network (
Fig. 3
). By contrast, the intein host protein and insertion site profiles of
A. flamelloides
and
A. ignava
are very different (
Fig. 2
and
Dataset S1
). Only eight orthologous insertion sites are shared between the two species [one in MCM8, one in DNA-directed RNA polymerase 1 subunit 1 (RPA1), one in DNA-directed RNA polymerase 3 subunit 2 (RPC2), two in Prp8, one in a Kinesin, one in a chromo domain-containing protein (SNF2), and one in the chromatin-remodeling protein HARP/SMARCAL1], and only five of 18 network clusters contain inteins from both species. This shows dramatic intein evolution since the two species diverged; it is unclear whether this is due primarily to differential intein acquisition or loss.
We analyzed the
A. ignava
and
A. flamelloides

Phylogenetic analysis shows that in the case of RPC2 (cluster 17), HE-lacking inteins found at orthologous sites in

A. ignava
and
A. flamelloides

Remarkably, this includes instances of intein spread to different locations within the same protein, spread among paralogous genes/proteins, and even between nonhomologous proteins. Such instances of intragenomic mobility are also apparent for inteins exclusive to each species.

Discussion
The spread of inteins between and within genomes is a long-standing puzzle in evolutionary biology. Often considered parasitic genetic elements (
6
), inteins are patchily distributed across the tree of life; when present, they reside in a restricted set of host proteins and only one or a few inteins are typically present in the genome of a given organism [note that some prokaryotic genomes have more than a dozen (
13
)]. We have shown that members of the newly described protist phylum Anaeramoebae harbor an exceptional abundance of intein-encoding regions in their nuclear genomes (103 in
A. ignava
), many of which appear to bend or break the “rules” of intein biology. Numerous novel intein host proteins were identified, including those in functional categories not known to harbor inteins in other organisms (e.g., cytoskeletal proteins and those involved in chromatin structure/dynamics). Taken as a whole, the intein content profiles of Anaeramoebae share similarities with both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, suggesting a role for LGT in their evolution and blurring the distinction between allelic and nonallelic homing.
As applied to inteins, the classical “homing cycle” of a parasitic element (
41
) begins with the acquisition of a HE-containing intein that spreads through a population by homing until no intein-lacking alleles remain. The HE then becomes inactive and disappears due to reduced selective pressure. The HE-free intein is lost and the empty site becomes a target for reinvasion. While appealing in its simplicity, this model ignores the obvious difficulty of intein loss, which must be very precise if the host protein is to retain functionality (
3
,
6
), and it does not specify how HE-bearing inteins are acquired in the first place (
14
,
18
,
42
). Our results support and greatly extend those of previous studies (
12
,
43
,
44
) in showing that LGT—within and between the three domains of life—can be an important source of inteins in eukaryotic nuclear genomes. In the case of
Anaeramoeba
, inteins appear to have come directly or indirectly from diverse prokaryotic sources. These anaerobic protists live in close association with diverse prokaryotes and a parallel study of the
Anaeramoeba
nuclear genome provides robust evidence for prokaryote-to-eukaryote LGT (
23
). Viruses are also clearly part of the
Anaeramoeba
intein picture. Some
Nucleocytoviricota
are thought to have a nuclear stage and thus could conceivably deliver intein donor alleles straight to the nucleus. The HE itself could also be encapsidated in a viral particle and delivered at the same time as intein donor DNA. The observation that several viral proteins with intein domains were detected in the CroV virion proteome of the protist
Cafeteria roenbergensis
(
45
) is in line with this possibility.
Most unexpected is the level of intein dynamism seen at the species level within
Anaeramoeba
. The intein distribution profiles of the three strains analyzed herein are exceedingly complex. Whereas some inteins are best explained as having been present in the common ancestor of
A. ignava
and
A. flamelloides
, many others are likely the product of more recent LGT. Having landed in the
Anaeramoeba
nuclear genome, many of these inteins appear to have spread to different locations within the same protein and to different proteins—both homologous and nonhomologous—with recent intron gain acting as a barrier to both allelic and nonallelic homing. At present we can only speculate as to how and why this has occurred. But it is noteworthy that unlike other Metamonada (
46
),
Anaeramoeba
spp. appear capable of NHEJ and have an unusual suite of DNA repair enzymes, many of which contain inteins (
SI Appendix
, section 10 and Fig. S15
). It may be that at least some of the HEs in Anaeramoebae are highly promiscuous, and/or that the protein machineries underlying homology-directed gene conversion (
4
,
5
) and/or NHEJ are unusually conducive to illegitimate intein homing. Regardless of the underlying reason(s), it remains to be seen whether Anaeramoebae are genuine outliers or represent the tip of an intein diversity iceberg. In any case, the promiscuous inteins described herein are of considerable practical use to protein biochemists working in the genetic engineering and biotechnology sectors (e.g., refs.
47
–
49
).
Materials and Methods
Intein Searches.
Two methods were used to detect inteins in the three
Anaeramoeba
predicted proteomes. First, BLAST (
50
) v2.9.0 was used (e-value <= 1e−5) with the inteins published in InBase and those described by Green et al. (
12
) as queries. Second, searches with Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) were performed using Hmmer (
51
) v. 3.3 using HMM profiles built using the N-terminal and C-terminal splicing domains of reference inteins (smart 00305, smart00306, PS50817, PS50818, PF14623, PF13403, and cd00081). Inteins detected during this first round of searching were used as queries for additional BLASTp searches. tBLASTn was used to detect potential pseudogenized inteins using the same queries as previously as well as the newly extracted complete set of
Anaeramoeba
full-length inteins.
Intein Splicing.
The splicing of inteins in
Anaeramoeba
was investigated experimentally using a combination of shotgun proteomics (
A. flamelloides
BUSSELTON2) and GFP-based in vitro expression analyses in
E. coli
(
A. ignava
BMAN). Detailed methodologies can be found in
SI Appendix
, section 2
. Proteomic data can be found in the PRoteomics IDEntifications (PRIDE) database (awaiting final access links).
Phylogenetic Analysis.
Unless specified otherwise, intein sequences were aligned with mafft (
52
) v7.407 using default parameters, sites were selected with bmge (
53
) v1.12 with the -m BLOSUM30 parameter, and IQ-TREE (
54
) v1.6.3 was used to reconstruct phylogenies with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates (
55
) under the C20+G4 mixture model.
Sequence Similarity Network.
Anaeramoeba
inteins were used as queries to retrieve homologous inteins from the
nr
database (2020). For each intein, the 25 best matching inteins were selected. The EFI EST software (
56
) was used to construct the network from the splicing domains of retrieved inteins using default parameters. For filtration into clusters, a threshold score corresponding to an average of 30% identity was used, which is an approximate threshold by which allelic and nonallelic inteins can be discriminated (
9
). The resulting network was visualized and edited with Cytoscape (
57
).
HE Domain Detection.
Two methods were used to detect HE domains, Interproscan v5.32-71.0 and HMM searches. In the latter case, HMM profiles constructed from alignments of HEs in the PFAM (PF00961, PF03161, PF05204, PF09062, PF10298, PF14527, PF14528, PF01223, PF01844, PF02945, PF03165, PF04231, PF05315, PF05551, PF05766, PF06147, PF07510, PF09230, PF12639, PF13391, PF13392, PF13395, PF13930, PF14279, PF14410, PF14411, PF14412, PF14414, PF16784, PF16786, and PF18275) and Prosite (PS50164) databases were used as queries.
DNA Replication and Repair Systems.
One hundred thirty-one human and yeast proteins from the replisome and NHEJ, HR, BER, NER, and MMR DNA repair pathways were used to identify their best PANTHER v15 family HMM model using PANTHER Score tool (
58
). These HMM models were then used to identify homologs in the predicted proteomes of the three
Anaeramoeba
genomes as well as those of
T. vaginalis
,
M. exilis
,
C. frisia
,
C. membranifera
,
K. bialata
,
G. intestinalis
WB,
S. salmonicida
,
N. gruberi
, and
D. discoideum
. Query proteins and retrieved homologs were then aligned with a random taxonomic sample from the same PANTHER family of interest for ortholog validation. Alignments were trimmed and subjected to phylogenetic reconstructions similarly to those described in ref.
46
.
